name: Sara Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two injection moulding machines at a plastics plant that makes dashboard clips and vent covers for car makers. I'm on nights this month, ten till six, so I clock in, check the moulds are hot, load the granules into the hopper and watch the parts drop. Every hour I pull a sample, check it against the gauge and log it on a paper sheet. Most of the job is listening, because a moulding machine tells you it's unhappy before the screen does.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I'm good at it without anyone standing over me. Nights are quiet, it's me, Dev on the next line and the radio. What wears me out is the heat off the barrels and the sleep, you never really sleep right on nights. And the rent on our flat went up again in spring, so the night premium isn't extra money anymore, it's just the rent.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Tomas, he drives a city bus. No kids yet. We've got about three months of bills in savings, which sounds okay until the boiler goes or the plant cuts a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read the card as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype. Okay, I can picture that one easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say I told you so, because the managers have been waving AI around in meetings for a year. In the union group chat I'd say good, now let's talk about pay instead of robots. I wouldn't post much online, I mostly just read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't make my life easy, it just leaves the old problems. The plant lost the vent cover contract to a cheaper plant last year and nights got cut from five to four for a while. Rent keeps climbing and pay doesn't. The night premium isn't extra money anymore, it's just the rent. So no AI doesn't mean no worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep my sample sheets clean, because clean records keep you safe when they pick who stays. I'd push the union rep, Marta, to fight for a proper pay rise at the next review in March. And I'd put fifty a month into savings, even if it means fewer takeaways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired more than scared. It's the same grind, just without the scary headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned nights were cut once. What happened that month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We lost about a fifth of my pay for six weeks. Tomas covered more of the rent and we ate a lot of pasta. I hated asking him, that's the part I remember.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the plant cut a shift again in this picture, what goes first in your budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym and the takeaways go first, then the trip to see my sister. The car stays, because there's no bus to the industrial estate at ten at night.

say: I'd tell the night crew the **AI hype** was just a story managers liked telling.
I'd say in the union chat that **pay**, not robots, is the real fight.
think: I think the **old pressures** stay: rent rising and a plant that already lost a contract.
I'm not safe just because AI fizzles; a **cut shift** still hurts us.
do: **Keep** sample sheets spotless so my record protects me when shifts get cut.
Push Marta, our rep, for a **pay rise** at the March review.
Save **fifty a month** by cutting takeaways.
feel: Mostly **tired**, the same grind without a scary headline on top.
S0.quote: The night premium isn't extra money anymore, it's just the rent.
fieldNote: Sara's worry comes from **rent** and a plant that already lost a contract, not from AI.
She remembers asking her partner for help with **shame** more than the money itself.
Her instinct is to lean on the **union** rather than change anything herself.

steps.text: Keep running both moulding machines on nights with clean sample sheets
Push the union rep for a pay rise at the March review
Put fifty a month into savings instead of takeaways

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read the card as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots more slowly. Right. That's the bit I'd notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office will feel it first, the schedulers and the buyers, and I'd feel bad for them. Out loud I'd say we need the union at the table before any new robot cell comes in. I'd probably share a petition or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared of the robot arms, not the software. They already put one pick-and-place arm on line six to pull parts out of the mould, and nobody on six got moved up, they just stopped replacing people who left. Slowly is still coming. My two machines are exactly the kind of thing an arm can tend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and get my name on the list for the new cell training, if there is one, even though I hate new screens. I'd move our savings into a separate account so we don't touch it. Tomas and I would put off the bigger flat we were looking at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like I can see the queue forming and I don't know where I'm standing in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you hate new screens but you'd sign up for the training. Which wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fear wins. I'd rather be bad at a screen than good at a job that's gone. I'd ask Dev to show me first, he's quicker with that stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older women on the assembly bench, the ones who've been there twenty years. They pack and inspect by hand, and that's exactly what the cameras do now.

say: I'd say the **union** must be at the table before any new robot cell arrives.
I'd say the **office staff** will feel the software first, and I'd mean it kindly.
think: I think the **robot arm** on line six is the real warning, not the software.
I believe they'll shrink us by **not replacing** people rather than firing anyone.
do: Go to every **union meeting** and push for a say on new robot cells.
Sign up for **cell training**, even though new screens make me nervous.
**Delay** the bigger flat and ring-fence our savings.
feel: **Anxious**, like a queue is forming and I don't know my place in it.
S1.quote: I'd rather be bad at a screen than good at a job that's gone.
fieldNote: Sara separates the **software** threat from the **robot arm** she can already see.
She's resistant to tech but fear pushes her toward **training** anyway.
Her concern for the older bench workers shows strong **solidarity**.

steps.text: Attend every union meeting about the new robot cells
Sign up for the robot cell training and ask Dev to coach her
Put off moving to the bigger flat with Tomas
Move savings into a separate account and leave it untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. I'll read the card as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before my lease is even up twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need government to step in, a wage guarantee or something. At work I'd say they'd better not use this as an excuse to sack people. Online I'd sign everything that says slow it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, the office goes in 2028 and that changes my job too, because the schedule and the quality checks come from a screen. Robots come for the moulding machines by 2031, and I'll be thirty-two with nothing else on my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all spending that isn't rent and food and get us to six months saved by the end of the first year. I'd ask the union to negotiate redundancy terms early, while the company still needs us. I'd look at the bus company where Tomas works, because driving might last a bit longer, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in my stomach. Five years sounds long, but not when you've got nothing lined up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas the night you heard about 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not having a baby until we know what we're living on. That would be a hard conversation, because we'd sort of planned for twenty-nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes how long I've got, not where I end up. In those three years I'd watch every single person whose work is on a screen get let go, and I'd know I'm next in line.

say: I'd demand a **wage guarantee** from government before companies sack people.
I'd sign every petition that tries to **slow it down**.
think: I think the **paperwork** side of my job goes in 2028 and the machine side by **2031**.
I'd be thirty-two with **nothing else** on my CV.
do: Cut to **rent and food** and reach six months saved within a year.
Push the union to settle **redundancy terms** early.
Ask about **bus driving** jobs where Tomas works.
feel: **Sick** in the stomach; five years feels short with **nothing lined up**.
S2.quote: Robots come for the moulding machines by 2031, and I'll be thirty-two with nothing else on my CV.
fieldNote: The three-year robot gap gives Sara **time**, but she sees no different **destination**.
Her **baby plans** are the first thing she'd put on hold.
She looks to **government** and the union, not to her own retraining.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and food to reach six months saved
Ask the union to negotiate redundancy terms early
Put off having a baby until income is clear
Ask at the bus depot about driver jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. I'll read the card as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, like the card says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say the government has to plan for this, retraining money and a proper safety net. At the union I'd want a campaign for a shorter working week, so the work gets shared out. I'd say it loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots by 2034 means I've got about seven years at the machines. That's long enough to get somewhere else, if I actually move. The trouble is, I know me, I'll wait until it's too late, because I hate changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a bus licence course, the company pays for it if you sign on. I'd keep the moulding job while I train. And I'd go with Marta to the regional union meetings about the shorter week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared but not frozen. Seven years is a real number, I can plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'll wait until it's too late. What would stop that happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas. He'd nag me, and he's right to. If he booked the test I'd turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you lose if you left the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, the radio, knowing exactly what a good part sounds like when it drops. I'm proud of that and nobody outside the plant knows it exists.

say: I'd say government needs **retraining money** and a real safety net.
I'd campaign for a **shorter working week** so the work is shared out.
think: I think robots by 2034 give me about **seven years** at the machines.
I'm afraid I'll **wait too long** because I hate changing.
do: Take the **bus licence** course the company pays for.
Keep the **moulding job** while I train.
Join Marta at the regional meetings on a **shorter week**.
feel: **Scared** but not frozen, because seven years is a number I can **plan** around.
S3.quote: I know me, I'll wait until it's too late, because I hate changing.
fieldNote: Sara names her own **resistance** as the main risk, which is unusually frank.
Her partner is the **push** she relies on to act.
She has real **pride** in a skill nobody outside the plant sees.

steps.text: Take the company-paid bus licence course in the first year
Join the union's regional campaign for a shorter working week
Keep running the moulding machines on nights while training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read the card as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's me at thirty-seven before robots, about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the government to get it right, so there's no excuse. At work I'd say let's use the time to write rules about who owns the robots. I'd be louder online than I am now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years means I'd probably stay at the plant for a good while. Robots around 2039 means I'm nearly forty before the machines go. That's both a relief and a trap, because it's easy to do nothing for eight years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving a bit and still get the bus licence, but slower, maybe in year two. I'd talk to Tomas about having a baby at twenty-nine like we planned. I'd stay in the union and push for retraining written into the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. It's still my job going, just further away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is ten years a trap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my mum stayed at the biscuit factory until it closed and then had nothing at fifty. Ten years felt like forever to her too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would retraining in the contract look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid hours every month to learn something, on the clock, not on my day off. If it's on my day off, I won't do it, I'm honest about that.

say: I'd say ten years leaves government **no excuse** to get it wrong.
I'd argue for rules about **who owns** the robots.
think: I think robots by 2039 let me stay until **nearly forty**.
I worry the long gap is a **trap** that lets me do nothing.
do: Get the **bus licence** in year two.
Go ahead with a **baby** at twenty-nine as planned.
Push for **paid retraining** hours written into the contract.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to breathe, since the loss is **further away**.
S4.quote: My mum stayed at the biscuit factory until it closed and then had nothing at fifty.
fieldNote: Her **mother's story** shapes how she reads a long warning.
She wants retraining **on the clock**, knowing she won't do it on days off.
Even with ten years she expects to **lose** the job, so she stays anxious.

steps.text: Get the bus licence in the second year
Plan a baby at twenty-nine with Tomas as first planned
Push for paid monthly retraining hours in the union contract

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. There's no time to be bad at something new before you have to be good at it. What would help is retraining paid on the clock and a wage guarantee while you switch, so I'm not choosing between rent and learning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. Nobody on the floor gets asked when a robot arm comes in. If I had a vote on that, I'd be a lot less scared.

headlineQuote: Nobody on the floor gets asked when a robot arm comes in.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old** injection moulding operator on nights at a car parts plastics plant.
She lives with Tomas, a **bus driver**, with about **three months** of savings and rising rent.
She dislikes new tech but **fear** would push her into training once robots come close.
She trusts the **union** and government more than managers to protect workers.
Her mood moves from uneasy in AI Plateau to **alarmed** in the faster AGI pictures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to learn something new before the job goes.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** on the clock and a **wage guarantee** while switching jobs.
